(Americanism Chairman Mrs. Melton) asks the FBI about a pamphlet, "Suicide or Murder?", which allegedly links Marilyn Monroe's death to a former Attorney General and mentions Communism. nodes.title: FBI Letter Declining Comment on Pamphlet, With Enclosures
nodes.summary: A January 26, 1965 FBI letter from Director J. Edgar Hoover to Mrs. Melton, Americanism Chairman of Mothers of World War I, Inc., replies to her January 20 inquiry. The FBI states it is an investigative agency that does not evaluate or judge the character or integrity of organizations, publications, or individuals, so it cannot comment on the pamphlet "Suicide or Murder?". It encloses five items: "Time for Decision," "Our Heritage of Greatness," "Faith in God--Our Answer To Communism," "Let's Fight Communism Sanely!," and an Internal Security Statement dated 4-17-62. Routing initials and a note reference appear.

The memo calls the rumors false, notes the alleged Los Angeles phone-tape claim is unsupported, and cites critical reviews from Time, the New York Times, and the Washington Post.

They add that Monroe realized he was not serious, and that Twentieth Century-Fox cancelled her contract amid Cleopatra-related financial trouble and replaced her mid-picture. Other garbled text covers her firing, her death in Brentwood, suicide attempts and psychiatric treatment, Peter Lawford, Dr. Greenson, phone records, a Life magazine article on Lawford's St. Francis Hotel and Soviet-related intelligence claims, a 1963 declassification guide, and Pentagon/Naval context. Routing slips list Bureau staff names.

summary: A June 11, 1956 FBI memo on Walter Winchell's broadcast claiming playwright Arthur Miller's divorce from Marilyn Monroe and a HUAC subpoena would probe his circle of former communist sympathizers. It notes Miller's communist-era ties, HUAC's request for him to testify, and that the Bureau lacked his CP card. A July 2, 1956 follow-up covers Winchell's claims of a Senate hearing on June 18 confronting labor leaders with Victor Riesel, Nasser's visit to Yugoslavia, and Miller's HUAC testimony refusing to name names.

title: FBI memo on Winchell broadcast, Miller testimony, and Khrushchev item
key_items: Winchell's broadcast was not carried locally on
summary: A July 2, 1956 internal FBI memo notes Walter Winchell's broadcast was not carried locally on station WWDC due to a baseball game, and reports items from his broadcast obtained from the New York Office. Winchell said a playwright's husband refused to name comrades at a committee hearing. Comment: Miller, a former CP member, testified before HUAC on 6/21/56, admitted attending 1939-40 CP writers' meetings and contributing to communist fronts, but refused to name names. A London 'Time and Tide' item reports Khrushchev may be released from Siberia. Marked for information.

nodes.title: Winchell Column Items on Algeria, HCUA Blacklisting Probe, and Cogley Report
nodes.summary: A memo to Mr. Boardman containing three items. A Winchell item reports the French government suffered depleted reserves in Algeria, with Washington and London fearing a general North African war by autumn; a comment marks it 'for information.' A second Winchell item says Dr. J. B. Matthews, former staff director of the McCarthy Senate committee, will testify July 10 as a star witness for HCUA's probe of a Fund for the Republic report alleging blacklisting, which Winchell says suppressed victims' communist records. A comment explains the report was a 1954 study funded by a $100,000 grant, written by John Cogley, and notes HCUA will question Cogley July 10, with FBI files showing no pertinent information on him.

nodes.title: WINGHELL SAID:
nodes.summary: A 1950s-60s FBI-style memo and newspaper excerpts. Walter Winchell comments on Arthur Miller's HUAC testimony: Miller claimed he quit Red front activity ten years earlier, but a pamphlet lists him as sponsor of the 1952 Citizens Emergency Defense Conference defending Smith Act victims; the group was later cited by the Attorney General. Hughes was acquitted of perjury tied to Matusow and misled Rauh and newspapers about McCarthy. Winchell also reports Communist Party leaders meeting secretly in Philadelphia and Boston Reds rejected by 22 law firms. Confidential magazine's libel conspiracy trial is covered: witnesses Virginia Lee, Frank Goldberg, Howard Rushmore and others describe paid informants and prostitute affidavits targeting Hollywood stars. A 1962 letter from the Bureau declines jurisdiction over a Marilyn Monroe newspaper item.
